kaigo-atomic-grooming-figure.heading: Reading shaving and nail-care illustrations
paragraphs: Facial hair affects the person’s appearance and preferences, so first ask how they would like it groomed. Observe their skin, check the instructions for the equipment and products, explain what you will do and obtain consent. Do not unilaterally choose the appearance that staff consider tidy.

The textbook’s electric-shaver illustration shows an example of holding the blade nearly perpendicular to the skin while stretching skin folds. It does not mean pressing hard to finish quickly. Do not apply a remembered angle alone to a device with a different blade or head structure; check the method specified for that product.

As you proceed, check the areas already shaved so that you notice missed areas and avoid unnecessary repeated shaving of the same spot. Also check the skin and how the person feels during use. Choose finishing products, such as moisturizers, that suit the skin, the person’s wishes and the plan. An example of skin lotion in the textbook is not an instruction to use the same product on everyone.

The nail illustration calls the example with a shaped tip “square-off” and distinguishes it from cutting too short or cutting diagonally into the sides. Read nail clippers and nail files as tools with different roles. Long or sharp nails can injure the skin, and dirt can collect around nails. Grooming aims to maintain cleanliness and protect skin; cutting deeper does not make a nail cleaner. Knowing the illustration’s terms does not establish that you may treat an abnormal nail.

Health conditions can affect nails, so observe changes in the nails and surrounding skin as well as length. Tell healthcare professionals about pain, redness, swelling or other abnormalities and confirm the method; do not diagnose a disease from nail appearance alone. The textbook discusses nails becoming softer after bathing, but softness or the person’s wish to hurry does not authorize you to treat an abnormal nail yourself. After cutting, smooth sharp areas with a nail file or similar tool within the appropriate scope.

[Learning example] You intend to use the angle learned on an earlier shaver with a new model. First check the model and handling instructions, the person’s skin and their wishes. Understanding an illustration is different from establishing that this device can be used safely with this person.

This explanation teaches the meaning of illustrations and terms and the reasons for assistance. Actual assistance must follow the person’s condition, individual care plan, product instructions and facility training. Do not try unfamiliar operations from text or pictures alone or record results that you have not confirmed.

kaigo-atomic-bed-wash-figures.heading: Connect body-washing areas, movements and warmth
paragraphs: Bed bathing cleans the body with warm towels or suitable cleansing products when, for example, a bath or shower is unsuitable. The material discusses stimulation of circulation and muscles as well as cleanliness, but stronger rubbing is not necessarily better. Match the method to the skin and the person’s responses. A full-body wash and a partial wash cover different areas. Do not assume consent to wash the entire body; check which areas the person wants help with and which method suits their current condition.

Prepare supplies so that clean items and used items remain separate. Work with areas such as the face, arms, chest and abdomen, back and legs individually. Treat intimate areas separately, paying attention to clean and contaminated areas and the scope of consent. The purpose goes beyond remembering an order: avoid spreading contamination while maintaining warmth and exposing only what is necessary. Check the method if it does not suit the person’s condition.

The material’s face-washing example starts around the eyes and also attends to the areas behind the ears and the neck. Arrows showing circular chest movements or movements along the back muscles indicate body areas and direction. Do not interpret horizontal lines around the shoulders, circular lines on the chest, abdomen and buttocks, and long lines on the back or sides as instructions for one identical movement.

The limb illustrations show an example of broad wiping movements using joints as reference points between areas. They do not show examining or wiping only around the joints. The material’s instruction to maintain steady pressure does not mean using the same force on everyone. Avoid strong rubbing on thin skin, wounds or painful areas, and check a method suited to the person’s responses, skin and available movement. Arrows alone do not determine force or repetitions.

After using a cleanser, check for and remove residue because remaining ingredients can cause itching. Damp skin loses heat easily, so promptly dry each area after washing it and cover it while working elsewhere. Exposing and wetting the entire body first and drying it all at the end may not maintain warmth or respect the person’s modesty to the same extent.

The material gives an example of preparing water hotter than bathwater because it cools during the task, with additional water available for adjustment. This does not mean that water in a container, a wet towel and the temperature at skin contact have identical conditions. Check a suitable temperature both during preparation and at use, using a method appropriate to the plan and equipment. Never apply the hot adjustment water directly to the person or carry it over their body. Do not reinterpret the example as meaning hotter is better.

[Learning example] The person wants only their arms washed. Even if full-body supplies are available, do not expand the scope; confirm the requested areas and method. Review preparation, washing, checking cleanser residue, drying and covering separately, considering each purpose and actual result.

This explanation teaches the meaning of illustrations and terms and the reasons for assistance. Actual assistance must follow the person’s condition, individual care plan, product instructions and facility training. Do not try unfamiliar operations from text or pictures alone or record results that you have not confirmed.

kaigo-atomic-adl-iadl.heading: Mobility connects daily activities and choices
paragraphs: When considering mobility support, ask what the person wants to do at the destination, not only where they want to move. Mobility connects with eating in the dining room, using the toilet, washing in the bathroom, socializing and many other daily activities. The range of activities a person can undertake also relates to physical and mental functions and participation in life.

Activities of daily living (ADL) are basic daily actions such as eating, dressing, bathing, toileting and moving around. Instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) include shopping, managing money, laundry and using transport or communication methods to organize home and community life. Do not use the category names alone to judge all of a person’s abilities.

Even activities with the same name, such as meal preparation, cleaning, laundry, organizing clothes, shopping and contacting others, differ according to personal habits and priorities. Check what the person decides and which parts they can perform, and direct assistance to the parts that need it. Being able to perform one ADL does not establish that every IADL is possible.

[Learning example] The person needs help moving in a wheelchair but manages their own budget and chooses what to buy. Do not transfer all shopping decisions to the family because mobility is limited. Confirm the person’s wishes and the parts they manage, then separately consider necessary help, such as getting to the store.

This explanation teaches the meaning of illustrations and terms and the reasons for assistance. Actual assistance must follow the person’s condition, individual care plan, product instructions and facility training. Do not try unfamiliar operations from text or pictures alone or record results that you have not confirmed.

kaigo-atomic-posture-names.heading: Check position names together with body support
paragraphs: Standing, sitting and lying are referred to as standing, seated and lying positions. Within seated positions, sitting in a chair, sitting at the edge of a bed with the legs down and sitting with the legs extended forward have different supporting surfaces and foot positions. Do not assume equal stability from the position name alone.

Supine means lying on the back, lateral means lying on the side and prone means lying face down. Right lateral means the person’s right side is underneath; do not substitute the right side seen by a worker facing them. Check which side of the body touches the supporting surface, not only which way the face points.

Taii means the body’s position, and taii henkan means changing that position. Shisei means posture or the way the body is held. In phrases such as “remain sitting at the bed edge,” “sit in a chair” and “move to standing,” distinguish the current state from the action of changing position.

The textbook’s supine example supports the body over a broad surface, but this alone does not make it best for everyone. Suitable support depends on pain, breathing, skin pressure and the person’s wishes. Names such as Fowler’s or semi-Fowler’s position do not prescribe one bed angle for everyone.

Lateral-position examples use cushions in front of the chest, under the lower leg or between the legs. The material’s semi-seated example raises the leg section of the bed, or supports the knees with a cushion if that section cannot be adjusted. The purpose is stability and avoidance of unnecessary pressure and sliding. Check the required cushion locations and thickness and skin contact according to the person and the equipment.

[Learning example] A record saying only “placed a pillow” does not establish what was supported or whether the person became comfortable. Record the supported body area and position, pain and breathing, the person’s own words and the results actually checked after adjustment. Do not equate a pillow’s presence with confirmed comfort.

This explanation teaches the meaning of illustrations and terms and the reasons for assistance. Actual assistance must follow the person’s condition, individual care plan, product instructions and facility training. Do not try unfamiliar operations from text or pictures alone or record results that you have not confirmed.

kaigo-atomic-disuse.heading: Check reduced activity and pressure risks separately
paragraphs: Prolonged rest or reduced activity can cause changes such as muscle wasting, joint stiffness and reduced bone, sensory or mental functions. These are studied as disuse syndrome. The term does not determine every function of a person merely from how long they spend lying down.

Cardiopulmonary function, blood-pressure regulation, internal-organ function, nutrition and activity capacity may also be affected. The illustration includes orthostatic hypotension, a fall in blood pressure on standing. Dizziness, palpitations or breathlessness on getting up should be observed and reported. However, do not attribute new symptoms simply to inactivity; arrange the necessary assessment.

Pressure injuries involve prolonged pressure, often over bony prominences, interfering with blood flow. According to posture, check skin and contact at the back of the head, shoulder-blade areas, elbows, sacral and buttock areas, heels and other relevant sites. One body area or one position does not establish that the whole body is free of risk.

Alongside pressure, review bedding creases, friction and body sliding. Smoothing creases matters, but it does not resolve prolonged pressure on one site. Consider how far the person can move independently, supporting surfaces, skin, activity, nutrition and other conditions together.

Combine possible activity and time out of bed, repositioning, pressure relief and nutrition support according to the person’s assessment and plan. Do not finish checking by applying one timetable to everyone; check their condition and responses afterward. Dressing and hygiene assistance also provide opportunities to observe skin. Report redness or other changes to healthcare professionals without waiting for a wound to develop.

The textbook’s example of releasing the back after raising the upper body illustrates reducing shear on back skin. Understanding this purpose does not authorize independently pulling or lifting the person. Confirm suitable equipment, methods and the helpers required, and use the method practiced in facility training.

[Learning example] The sheet is flat, but the heel has remained in contact with the same spot for a long time. Do not conclude that no pressure-injury risk exists because there are no creases. Check the heel’s skin and contact and how the person feels, then confirm the support method in the plan and any necessary reporting.

This explanation teaches the meaning of illustrations and terms and the reasons for assistance. Actual assistance must follow the person’s condition, individual care plan, product instructions and facility training. Do not try unfamiliar operations from text or pictures alone or record results that you have not confirmed.

kaigo-atomic-movement-devices.heading: Distinguish equipment purposes and component roles
paragraphs: Canes, walkers and lifts all relate to mobility, but their support purposes and conditions of use differ. A T-handle cane is relatively light and easy to handle, while a multi-point cane has a wider base of support. The material gives reduced lower-limb stability or strength as an example for using a multi-point cane, but that condition alone does not establish suitability. Walkers also increase support, yet base width alone cannot rank suitability for everyone. Check the person’s movements, location of use, equipment and professional assessment together.

Mobility lifts include ceiling-track and floor-based models used to support the body during transfers. Correct use of suitable equipment can reduce strain on the person and care workers. Knowing a model name does not establish ability to use it; check the person’s condition, product requirements and handling training. Do not make manual lifting the default for people needing full assistance.

A wheelchair’s drive wheel and hand rim are different. The rear wheel supports and moves the body as a wheel; the hand rim outside it is handled by the person when propelling themselves. Push handles are for the helper. Their presence alone does not establish whether the person can propel the wheelchair.

The back support, seat, arm support, leg support and foot support respectively support the back, sitting area, arms, lower legs and feet. Distinguish the front casters too. Do not use foot supports as steps for standing on during entry or exit.

Parking brakes and helper-operated brakes near the push handles have different roles. Apply parking brakes when stopped, even without an occupant, and check the tires and braking effectiveness before use. Low tire pressure can prevent parking brakes from holding sufficiently. Do not end the inspection by looking only at lever position.

A tipping lever is used, for example, to raise or lower front wheels through a trained operation suited to the model’s design. Knowing its location does not authorize trying an unfamiliar curb maneuver. If the equipment is faulty or handling is unclear, stop using it and seek clarification.

Distinguish movement terms too. Ido means changing location; ijo means transferring between supporting places, such as bed and wheelchair. Okiagaru means raising the upper body from lying, while negaeri means turning while lying. Gasho and risho distinguish lying in bed from getting out of bed.

A sliding sheet reduces friction, unlike a lift that suspends the body or a walker that supports walking. For a senior shopping walker or trolley, check the model, the person’s ability and the product’s intended use; do not assume it can replace a walking frame or passenger wheelchair. A white cane relates to visual impairment. Do not assume it serves the same purpose as a weight-supporting cane selected by its number of legs.

In “bureki o kakeru,” kakeru means applying the brake; in “tsue o tsuku,” tsuku means placing the cane on the ground for support. Tsukamaru means holding a support, nigiru means grasping with the hand, and sasaeru means providing necessary support to a body or object. An isolated word meaning does not establish the action without context.

Koekake means verbally explaining, checking or otherwise communicating with the other person. Yudo means guiding them along a route or similar path in a way suited to them. Reading these terms does not remove the need to explain, obtain consent, inspect equipment or train in its use.

[Learning example] Someone intends to choose a cane on the assumption that more legs make it best for everyone. A wider base is one feature, but selection must also consider the person’s movement, location of use, ease of handling and the method taught to them.

This explanation teaches the meaning of illustrations and terms and the reasons for assistance. Actual assistance must follow the person’s condition, individual care plan, product instructions and facility training. Do not try unfamiliar operations from text or pictures alone or record results that you have not confirmed.

kaigo-atomic-turning-sitting.heading: Read the conditions for turning and sitting up
paragraphs: Before changing position, check current physical condition, pain and available movement, explain what will happen and obtain consent. Prepare the required equipment, staff, space and bed height. If the person feels unwell, do not prioritize the schedule and continue; tell the necessary recipient, such as a healthcare professional.

Using a person with left hemiplegia as one example, the textbook discusses turning onto the side with the paralyzed side uppermost. Bending the knees and gathering the body within the person’s ability makes turning easier. Use the parts they can perform themselves; do not pull the paralyzed arm to move the whole body.

After turning, the source example adjusts the pelvis and lower back backward and positions the legs comfortably to establish stable side-lying support. Gathering the body to make movement easier and increasing support afterward serve different purposes. Do not read “make the body compact” and “increase support” as contradictory instructions for the same moment. Specific positions and movements must suit the person’s condition, individual care plan and trained method.

The textbook’s sitting-up example moves from right side-lying, brings both legs to the bed edge and down, and uses the right elbow for support while raising the upper body into sitting at the bed edge. It illustrates coordination of legs, trunk and supporting points, with the right elbow as the illustrated support. It does not instruct everyone to use the right elbow or one identical arm movement. Follow the person’s available strength and movement, individual plan and practical training.

Adjusting the bed to a suitable working height aims to reduce the care worker’s back strain. For sitting at the bed edge, however, arrange suitable support for both soles on the floor or another surface. Purposes change between stages; a suitable working height is not necessarily suitable for the person’s sitting position.

After repositioning, check pain, how the person feels, dizziness, foot support and balance. Completion of sitting up does not establish that they can sit steadily or proceed to standing or a transfer. If the method is unclear or their condition differs, seek the necessary help before starting the next movement.

[Learning example] You intend to move the knees and legs of a person with restricted hip movement in the same way as the left-hemiplegia example. Do not decide applicability from a diagnosis or diagram orientation alone. Check the individual assessment, possible movements, plan and trained method. Understanding the illustration’s purpose differs from establishing that the conditions for performing it with this person are met.

This explanation teaches the meaning of illustrations and terms and the reasons for assistance. Actual assistance must follow the person’s condition, individual care plan, product instructions and facility training. Do not try unfamiliar operations from text or pictures alone or record results that you have not confirmed.

99.title: Read shaving and nail illustrations with their conditions
objectives: Distinguish illustrated movements from product-specific and individual conditions.
Check grooming preferences and skin and nail condition, and refer abnormalities to healthcare professionals.
99.context: Consider whether a remembered angle can be used unchanged with another shaver type. Distinguish understanding the illustration, checking the product and obtaining the person’s consent.
99.artCaption: A clothing-choice scene highlights the importance of checking wishes during grooming too. It is not a shaving or nail-cutting technique diagram.

100.title: Understand why bed bathing proceeds by body area
objectives: Connect cleanliness, warmth and exposure with the area being washed.
Distinguish movement direction from force, and check drying and covering afterward.
100.context: Consider whether wetting the whole body and drying everything last is equivalent to working area by area. Also check whether the person wants a full or partial wash.
100.artCaption: Prepare bed-bathing supplies and surroundings. Water and towels alone do not establish suitable temperature, cleanliness or completed assistance.

101.title: Consider mobility, ADL and IADL through daily-life purposes
objectives: Explain how mobility supports participation in daily life.
Check abilities and assistance needs separately for each activity.
101.context: Using a person who needs wheelchair mobility support but manages their own money, distinguish mobility assistance from shopping decisions. Practice avoiding assumptions that the family should manage everything.
101.artCaption: Discuss the dressing movements the person performs and the help needed. Do not infer other daily-life abilities from one action.

102.title: Check posture names and supporting locations
objectives: Distinguish position names and orientation from actions that change position.
Check comfort and the result of support, beyond the presence of cushions.
102.context: Consider whether “placed a pillow” alone establishes a comfortable position. Distinguish the supported area, pressure, the person’s words and results actually checked.
102.artCaption: A chair and a bed provide different body and foot support. Check actual conditions as well as the position name.

103.title: Consider disuse and pressure risks from several perspectives
objectives: Distinguish changes associated with reduced activity from assumptions about causes.
Check pressure, skin, activity and nutrition as well as bedding creases.
103.context: Consider what to check for someone remaining in the same position after bedding creases are smoothed. This is not a situation for diagnosing every new symptom as disuse.
103.artCaption: Care workers and healthcare professionals discuss posture, supporting surfaces and skin observations. The picture alone cannot establish effective pressure relief.

104.title: Distinguish equipment features, parts and purposes
objectives: Explain the purposes and suitability of canes, walkers and lifts.
Check wheelchair inspection points and distinguish mobility and transfer terms.
104.context: Consider whether a multi-point cane’s wider base makes it best for everyone. Practice combining individual, environmental and product conditions when selecting equipment.
104.artCaption: Staff check the purposes and individual suitability of equipment. A picture showing equipment does not establish safe handling.

105.title: Read turning and sitting-up examples with individual conditions
objectives: Separate making movement easier from stabilizing posture afterward.
Check condition, possible movements, foot support and the person’s condition after assistance.
105.context: Consider whether a textbook example of left hemiplegia can be applied unchanged to another person with restricted hip movement. Individual assessment and a trained method are needed first.
105.artCaption: Check the individual plan and roles before turning or sitting up. A background conversation does not prove practical assistance is complete.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-grooming-figure.prompt: You intend to apply a remembered illustration angle unchanged to a shaver with a different structure. What must be checked?
options: All electrically powered devices use the same angle and force.
If the person wants grooming, checking device handling is unnecessary.
Press hard against the skin first and read instructions only if redness appears.
Check the product model and instructions, the person’s skin and wishes, the plan and consent before choosing a method.
rationales: Even with the same electric-shaver name, each product’s structure and instructions need checking.
Wishes and consent matter but are separate from checking proper device handling.
Check suitable methods and condition before use, rather than after putting strain on skin.
This checks product-specific and individual conditions instead of generalizing an example unconditionally.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-bed-wash-figure.prompt: You intend to expose and wet the whole body first, then dry everything at the end during bed bathing. Which approach is appropriate?
options: If wiping direction is correct, exposure and time spent wet do not matter.
Consent to a wash allows expansion to the whole body even if only a partial wash is wanted.
Check cleanliness and cleanser residue area by area, then dry and cover. For intimate areas, also check scope and clean–dirty separation.
After cleanser use, leaving ingredients on the skin is always cleaner.
rationales: Warmth and privacy for wet or exposed skin need attention separately from movement direction.
Confirm the scope of consent; do not expand the areas the person wants washed without permission.
This avoids prolonged wide exposure while wet and considers warmth, cleanliness and modesty.
Cleanser residue can burden skin, so check and appropriately remove it.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-adl-iadl.prompt: The person needs wheelchair mobility assistance but manages their own budget. Which shopping support is appropriate?
options: Check their wishes and the parts they manage, then assist where needed, such as mobility.
Let the family decide all shopping for anyone using a wheelchair.
Managing money means mobility assistance is unnecessary too.
Staff choose convenient stores and products and tell the person after purchase.
rationales: This does not infer lost shopping judgment or money-management ability from mobility limitations.
Needing mobility help differs from being able to decide what to buy.
One IADL ability cannot cancel support needed for another action.
This replaces the person’s life choices with staff convenience.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-posture-names.prompt: A record says only “placed a pillow.” Can you say the person is comfortably positioned?
options: A pillow removes pain wherever it is placed.
Adding the name Fowler’s position establishes that support results were checked.
If the posture looks tidy to staff, asking how the person feels is unnecessary.
Not yet. Check the supported area and location, pressure, the person’s words and their condition after adjustment.
rationales: A pillow’s presence does not prove suitable positioning or absence of pain.
A posture name does not prove actual condition or support was checked.
Appearance alone cannot establish pain, breathing or how the person feels.
Check the placement fact separately from whether suitable support made the person comfortable.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-disuse.prompt: You smoothed the sheet of someone who stays in one position for a long time. Which understanding of pressure-injury risk is appropriate?
options: Without creases, prolonged pressure at one site is harmless.
Smoothing creases alone is insufficient; check pressure, shear, skin, activity, nutrition and the plan.
Do not report redness until the skin breaks open.
All new dizziness and breathlessness can be diagnosed as inactivity.
rationales: Smoothing creases does not remove every condition causing prolonged pressure.
Bedding creases are one condition; check other factors and the person’s condition too.
Report redness and other changes to healthcare professionals for assessment without waiting for a wound.
Even if reduced activity can be related, do not independently decide the cause of new symptoms.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-movement-device.prompt: Someone says a multi-point cane is better for everyone because its base of support is wider. Which correction is appropriate?
options: Base width is one feature; check abilities, environment, equipment suitability and the method taught.
With more cane legs, there is no need to check whether the person can handle it.
Walkers and white canes have the same purpose and can be selected by shape alone.
Knowing cane types removes the need for handling training or a plan.
rationales: Consider actual use conditions rather than ranking equipment from one shape feature alone.
Safe handling matters; base width alone does not establish suitability.
Purposes and supporting conditions differ, so shape alone does not establish identical use.
Knowing names does not replace suitability checks, handling training or the individual care plan.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-turning-sitting.prompt: You intend to apply a left-hemiplegia textbook example unchanged to someone else with restricted hip movement. Which approach is appropriate?
options: The same position name means moving identically regardless of joint restrictions.
Memorizing the illustration order allows omission of explanation and consent.
Check their assessment, available movement, plan and trained method rather than directly applying the illustrated movements.
Once sitting up is complete, ask them to stand without checking foot support or dizziness.
rationales: Even with the same position name, available movement and suitable support need individual checking.
Knowledge of a procedure does not remove the need to check understanding and consent.
One conditional example cannot determine the same method for someone with different joint conditions.
Completing sitting up differs from stable sitting; check condition before proceeding.
